Code checkout on the host:
Nothing in this list has run against AWS. Each apply is the owner's. The list is for an existing installation: the code one-shot task definition (the family whose name ends in `_code_fetch`) is already registered, because `host_session start --code-run` refuses before the host turns on when it is not. A fresh stack, where it is not registered yet, needs a first registration that this list does not cover. Show the plan first and apply exactly that plan. Run every command from the repository root of the main checkout. The list puts the reviewed code of one run on the host as `/data/repo`, the checkout that Airflow and the OpenMetadata bootstrap mount. Run every block of this list in one shell, so the variables that an earlier block sets stay set for the later blocks. The first block sets them. It makes the one new folder under the ignored `plans/` folder that holds every file this list saves (`RECORD_DIR`), reads the project profile and the region from `.env` with the project's own dotenv parser, reads the data bucket name from the storage stack and asks for the administrator profile. Read the printed values and stop if one is empty:

```sh
RECORD_DIR="plans/code_checkout_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mkdir -p "$RECORD_DIR"
PROJECT_PROFILE="$(.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.project_setting aws_profile)"
REGION="$(.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.project_setting aws_region)"
DATA_BUCKET="$(terraform -chdir=infra output -raw bucket_name)"
printf 'Administrator profile: '
read -r ADMIN_PROFILE
printf '%s %s %s %s %s\n' "$RECORD_DIR" "$PROJECT_PROFILE" "$REGION" "$DATA_BUCKET" "$ADMIN_PROFILE"
```

1. `infra/iam` (administrator profile): set `host_code_fetch_prepared` to `true` in `config/aws/iam_preparation.json`. The file stays on your machine and is never committed. The plan must add the role `host_code_fetch_task` and its one policy `code_archive_read`, which allows `s3:GetObject` on `lakehouse/run_stage/*/inputs/code.tar.gz` and nothing else. Stop on any other change. Show the plan:

   ```sh
   IAM_PLAN="$PWD/$RECORD_DIR/iam.tfplan"
   bash scripts/infrastructure/terraform.sh --iam --admin-profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" plan -out "$IAM_PLAN"
   ```

   Apply exactly that plan, then save the role in the record folder and read it:

   ```sh
   bash scripts/infrastructure/terraform.sh --iam --admin-profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" apply "$IAM_PLAN"
   terraform -chdir=infra/iam output -json host_code_fetch_role > "$RECORD_DIR/host_code_fetch_role.json"
   cat "$RECORD_DIR/host_code_fetch_role.json"
   ```

   Then apply the project user's policy (administrator profile). The project user can pass only the roles that its policy lists, and the services apply of step 5 registers the code one-shot task definition with this role, so the policy file now lists `host_code_fetch_task`. Without this apply, the `RunTask` call of the code one-shot in step 4 and `RegisterTaskDefinition` in step 5 are refused. Show the plan, then apply with the typed confirmation and the `Plan digest` the reviewed plan printed (apply changes nothing if the templates or the live policies changed since that plan). The plan must change the `iam` policy to add the role. Stop and ask on any other change you did not expect. Keep the output of the plan:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m infra.iam.scripts.manage_policies plan --admin-profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" | tee "$RECORD_DIR/policy_plan.txt"
   ```

   Then apply it. The first command reads the `Plan digest` that the plan printed from the saved output:

   ```sh
   PLAN_DIGEST="$(sed -n 's/^Plan digest: //p' "$RECORD_DIR/policy_plan.txt")"
   CONFIRM_IAM_POLICIES=apply-healthcare-hai-prediction-policies .venv/bin/python -m infra.iam.scripts.manage_policies apply --admin-profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" --digest "$PLAN_DIGEST"
   ```

2. Images (project profile): the code one-shot runs the training image, which carries the fetch script of the training task. Its digest must be in the services image digests. Print the plan of the build and push and run the printed commands if the training image is not pushed yet:

   ```sh

   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.push_images plan --repository-urls "$RECORD_DIR/repository_urls.json" --profile "$PROJECT_PROFILE" --region "$REGION" --only training
   ```

3. Stage the code (project profile). The first command makes a new run ID. The archive comes from `scripts.lakehouse.code_archive`, which adds the verified dbt packages. The code digest is the content of `code.sha256`, and the last two commands read it into `CODE_SHA256` and print both values:

   ```sh
   RUN_ID="$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-$(openssl rand -hex 4)"
   CODE_DIR="/tmp/code_$RUN_ID"
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.lakehouse.code_archive build --output "$CODE_DIR"
   aws s3 cp "$CODE_DIR/code.tar.gz" "s3://$DATA_BUCKET/lakehouse/run_stage/$RUN_ID/inputs/code.tar.gz" --profile "$PROJECT_PROFILE" --region "$REGION"
   aws s3 cp "$CODE_DIR/code.sha256" "s3://$DATA_BUCKET/lakehouse/run_stage/$RUN_ID/inputs/code.sha256" --profile "$PROJECT_PROFILE" --region "$REGION"
   CODE_SHA256="$(cat "$CODE_DIR/code.sha256")"
   ```

4. Start the host with that code (project profile). Apply the services stack only while the host runs: with no instance, the ECS deployment circuit breaker rolls every service back. After `host_prepare` the code one-shot downloads the archive, checks it against the digest, unpacks it into a private folder, renames that folder to a folder of `/data/repo_releases/` named by the code digest only when it holds every file of the archive and only then points `/data/repo` at it. A second code task then checks that `/data/repo` shows that release and that the release holds every file of its archive. When a code task fails, a third task makes `/data/repo` show a verified checkout again, and the start names what it shows. The services start after it, so they mount the new checkout. A refused or failed fetch keeps the previous checkout and stops the start before any service. Repeating the start with the same code changes nothing. A later start without `--code-run` keeps the checkout, and it fails on a host that has none:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.host_session start --code-run "$RUN_ID" --code-sha256 "$CODE_SHA256"
   ```

The services renderer treats this file as the whole set of nondefault services inputs, so a file that holds only the code one-shot role and the bucket would reset every other setting, such as `mlflow_enabled`, to its default. The tool keeps every setting that a services preparation file supports, sets `code_fetch_task_role_arn` to the role of step 1 and `code_bucket_name` to the data bucket, checks the result against the preparation schema and prints setting names only. Read the printed names and then the file: `kept` must list every nondefault services setting that you run today. The tool stops and names a setting that the services stack declares and no preparation file can carry. Stop and ask in that case. The plan must change at most the code one-shot task definition (the family whose name ends in `_code_fetch`) and nothing else. A plan that shows another change means a setting was lost from the file: do not apply it. The `shasum` command puts the complete file's SHA-256 in `SERVICES_INPUTS_SHA256`, and the plan and the apply both use it:

   ```sh
   printf '%s\n' "$DATA_BUCKET" > "$RECORD_DIR/data_bucket.txt"
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.services_code_inputs --existing infra/services/deployment.auto.tfvars.json --role-file "$RECORD_DIR/host_code_fetch_role.json" --bucket-file "$RECORD_DIR/data_bucket.txt" --output "$RECORD_DIR/services_code.json"
   cat "$RECORD_DIR/services_code.json"
   SERVICES_INPUTS_SHA256="$(shasum -a 256 "$RECORD_DIR/services_code.json" | cut -d' ' -f1)"
   printf '%s\n' "$SERVICES_INPUTS_SHA256"
   SERVICES_PLAN="$PWD/$RECORD_DIR/services.tfplan"
   bash scripts/infrastructure/terraform.sh --services --preparation-inputs "$RECORD_DIR/services_code.json" --preparation-sha256 "$SERVICES_INPUTS_SHA256" plan -out "$SERVICES_PLAN"
   ```

   Apply exactly that plan:

   ```sh
   bash scripts/infrastructure/terraform.sh --services --preparation-inputs "$RECORD_DIR/services_code.json" --preparation-sha256 "$SERVICES_INPUTS_SHA256" apply "$SERVICES_PLAN"
   ```

   The services apply first takes the apply lock, so no other services apply starts, then sets the launch hold before it changes anything. While the lock exists or the hold is set, no host job launches. It clears the hold and deletes its own lock only after the ECS services reach steady state. If the apply, the hold write or that wait fails, the lock (and the hold, when it was set) stay, and the failure prints a resolve command. Do not paste that command: it holds a placeholder where your statement belongs. Check the apply and the services. The `apply lock:` line of `status` shows the token of the lock that the failed apply holds:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.services_apply status
   ```

   Then clear the hold and the lock. The block asks for what you checked and for that token and passes both as you typed them:

   ```sh
   printf 'What you checked: '
   read -r RESOLVE_STATEMENT
   printf 'Token of the failed apply lock: '
   read -r LOCK_TOKEN
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.services_apply resolve --statement "$RESOLVE_STATEMENT" --token "$LOCK_TOKEN"
   ```

   A new code one-shot revision from this apply does not change `/data/repo` now: the checkout of step 4 stays, and the next host start runs the new revision. To use it now, run step 4 again with the same run ID.

6. To move to newer code, repeat steps 3 and 4 with a new run ID. A running Airflow keeps the checkout it started with until the next start. Stop the host when the session ends:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.host_session stop
   ```

Nothing in this list has run against AWS. Run every command from the repository root of the checkout whose code the host runs. The list runs the first silver publish and then the first gold publish through the Airflow of the host. Each DAG step launches its job as one ECS task on the host through the direct ECS launch, so no step starts a Fargate task and no step starts a task by hand. Silver runs first because the gold step needs the silver launch record that the silver run writes. The list starts from this state: the jobs stack registered the host twins `<PROJECT_NAME>_<ENVIRONMENT>_job_silver_host` and `<PROJECT_NAME>_<ENVIRONMENT>_job_gold_host`, the services stack runs the Airflow scheduler as the launch role with the data bucket as `airflow_launch_bucket_name` and the host runs the reviewed code of "Code checkout on the host". The evidence task of each DAG run writes the acceptance report itself, so the owner approves no run ID and signs nothing. The host stays on for both runs and the owner stops it once at the end. `host_session stop` waits for desired capacity 0 and no group instance and records `host_off_verified`, which is the proof that the host is stopped. Keep every file this list saves in one new folder under the ignored `plans/` folder. The list calls it `<RECORD_DIR>`.

The Airflow pool `host_jobs` has one slot after each host start, because the migrate container sets it at every service start. So one host job runs at a time. Today no repository command changes the pool: the list drains by waiting for each run to end, not by setting the pool to 0 slots. Every stop condition below goes to step 10, which ends the session safely. Never leave the host on after a failure.

3. Stage the code for the silver run (project profile). Choose a new run ID for silver. The direct launch reads the code of a run from `lakehouse/run_stage/<run>/inputs/`, so each run needs its own staged copy before its trigger. Without it the step waits 10 minutes and fails with `code_digest_not_staged`. The archive comes from `scripts.lakehouse.code_archive`, which adds the verified dbt packages. The code digest is the content of `code.sha256`. Stop if the build refuses and go to step 10:

   ```sh

   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.lakehouse.code_archive build --output /tmp/code_<SILVER_RUN_ID>
   ```

4. Run silver through the DAG (project profile). `trigger_dag` reads the Airflow token secret from Parameter Store, signs a short token and calls the forwarded port. It unpauses `silver_transform_dag`, starts the run, waits at most 4 hours and writes one line of JSON with the end state and the state of every task. It exits 0 only for the state `success`. HTTP 401 means that the token secret changed after the services started: a start of the local Airflow writes a new `airflow_jwt_secret` to the same parameter. Start no local Airflow during the session. The job task saves the listing of all object versions under `lakehouse/` in the scheduler container after it holds the pool slot and right before the launch, so the writes of another run during the wait are in the listing and not in this run's writes. Right after the launch, while it still holds the slot, the job task saves the closing evidence in the same folder: the listing after the launch, the tasks of the job family that still run and the host facts, so the job that takes the slot next cannot change them. The evidence task then reads the records of the run and writes the acceptance report in the scheduler container. It binds the run to the staged code digest and to the launch records, and it keeps every check of the first publish acceptance. The DAG fails if one check fails, and the log of the evidence task holds the report with each check and the SHA-256 of each file it read. The evidence task also fails when the saved listing or the closing evidence is missing, damaged, readable by others or belongs to another run, for example after a scheduler restart, and a retry with a report on disk checks the saved listing again. Then the run needs a new run ID. Stop if the command exits with any other code than 0 and go to step 10:

   ```sh
   .venv/bin/python -m scripts.orchestration.trigger_dag --dag silver_transform_dag --mode real --run-id <SILVER_RUN_ID> --wait-seconds 14400 > <RECORD_DIR>/dag_silver.json
   ```

5. Keep the silver records (project profile). The silver step writes the write-once records of its launch under `lakehouse/launch_records/<SILVER_RUN_ID>/silver/`: the claim, then the intent, started and end records of the attempt. The end record must have the outcome `succeeded`. The run records are under `lakehouse/layer_runs/silver/<SILVER_RUN_ID>/`. Stop if the end record is missing or not `succeeded` and go to step 10:

   ```sh

   aws s3 cp s3://<DATA_BUCKET>/lakehouse/layer_runs/silver/<SILVER_RUN_ID>/ <RECORD_DIR>/evidence_silver/ --recursive --exclude '*' --include '*.json' --profile <PROJECT_PROFILE> --region <REGION>
   ```

Its step refuses before any ECS call unless `lakehouse/launch_records/<SILVER_RUN_ID>/silver/` holds the ended silver launch of step 5 with the outcome `succeeded`. Its evidence task also needs the silver report that the silver evidence task wrote in the same scheduler container and fails when that report is missing or belongs to another run. HTTP 401 has the cause of step 4. Stop if the command exits with any other code than 0 and go to step 10:

8. Keep the gold records as in step 5 (project profile), with the records under `lakehouse/launch_records/<GOLD_RUN_ID>/gold/` and `lakehouse/layer_runs/gold/<GOLD_RUN_ID>/`. Stop if the end record is missing or not `succeeded` and go to step 10:

10. If a step fails or a wait ends (project profile). This path ends the session safely. It does not repair the run. `trigger_dag` creates the Airflow run before it waits, so a failed trigger can leave a queued or running run that the scheduler starts again at the next host start. Run this path for the run of the failed step, with its DAG in place of `<DAG_ID>` and its run ID in place of `<RUN_ID>`:
    - Copy the run's launch records. An end record gives the outcome. A started record without an end record means that the job task may still run. No record means that the launch state is unconfirmed: the run may still be queued and launch its job later.
    - Read the run's state over the forward, then settle it. If the forward is closed, open it again as in step 2. `--status` changes nothing. `--settle` pauses the DAG, marks a run that has not ended failed and reads it again until it ends, within 10 minutes. The settle has worked when it exits 0 and prints the state `failed`, `success` or `absent`. `absent` means that Airflow holds no such run.
    - If Airflow cannot be reached, so that the status or the settle exits 1, set a restart hold. Choose a new run ID as `<HOLD_RUN_ID>` and stage nothing under it. Bind the run to it: its job step then finds no code digest, fails after 10 minutes with `code_digest_not_staged` and starts no ECS task. Add the run to `<RECORD_DIR>/restart_hold.txt`. The next session settles it right after its forward opens (step 2).
    - List the job tasks. While one runs, list again every 15 minutes for at most 2.5 hours after the `trigger_dag` wait ended. The job deadline is 6 hours from its start. The launch stops its task at the deadline. If a job task still runs after that bound, stop it with `aws_tasks stop`. A stopped attempt needs a new run ID. List again: the listing must show that it names no job task.
    - An unfinished launch needs no step while its task can be found. When the copied records of the job hold a claim but no end record, the next run of the family cancels the launch at its launch gate. That ends it when its task is found by identity and shows STOPPED, or when no ECS call was ever sent. If a call may have been sent and no task is found, nothing ends the launch: not the send window of the claim (10 minutes after the `at` of the claim record) and not an empty listing, because ECS lists a new task late and a request can still be in flight. The same holds when the copied records hold a task ARN in `started.json` that ECS no longer describes (ECS keeps a stopped task for at least one hour), because no stop can then be confirmed. That run is then refused with FamilyBusy and the reason, which names the old run, job and attempt, the task tag and, when saved, the task ARN. Stop every job task first, so the listing above names no job task, and start a new run once ECS lists the task and shows it STOPPED. If the refusal says that a launch record could not be read or written, it may be temporary: start the run again. If no task ever appears, or ECS never describes the saved task as STOPPED, leave the host stopped, keep the copied records and ask the owner: no command in this list ends that launch.
    - End the forward with Ctrl-C in the second terminal, if it is open.
    - Stop the host and check that the status names no instance. A failed run needs a new run ID, and the next gold run reads only a passed silver report.

Code staging setup on GitHub:
Nothing in this block has run. It sets up the GitHub side of the code-staging workflow with your signed-in `gh`: the `code-staging` environment (no reviewers, no wait timer, deployments from `main` only) and the repository variables `CODE_RUN_PARAMETER`, `AWS_REGION` and `OIDC_DELIVERY_ENABLED`. Nothing is typed: the project name and the region come from `.env`, and the repository and the delivery flag come from the output `github_oidc_contract` of the IAM stack, read with the profile in `.env`. It reads everything back and stops with a failing line if any part differs. It changes nothing it already has, so you can run it again. The output names each part and masks the bucket, the profile, the project and the region. Run it from any folder of the main checkout, in zsh or bash, after the IAM stack that creates the staging role is applied.

1. Set up the environment and the variables, then read them back. The last line says whether every part matches:

```sh
zsh <<'OWNER_BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'print -u2 -- "Stopped at line $LINENO. Read the line above, fix it and run the block again: it changes nothing it already has."; exit 1' ERR
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
value() {
  local line
  line="$(grep -E "^$1=" .env | head -n 1 || true)"
  [[ -n "$line" ]] || { print -u2 -- "$1 is not in .env"; return 1; }
  line="${line#*=}"; line="${line#\"}"; print -r -- "${line%\"}"
}
region="$(value AWS_REGION)"
profile="$(value AWS_PROFILE)"
bucket="$(value S3_BUCKET)"
project="$(value PROJECT_NAME)"
mask() { sed -e "s|$bucket|<bucket>|g" -e "s|$profile|<profile>|g" -e "s|$project|<project>|g" -e "s|$region|<region>|g"; }
gh auth status > /dev/null 2>&1 || { print -u2 -- "gh is not signed in: run gh auth login first"; exit 1; }
AWS_PROFILE="$profile" .venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.github_code_staging_bootstrap 2>&1 | mask
OWNER_BLOCK
```

2. Open the repository's Settings, then Environments, and look at `code-staging`: it must show no required reviewers, no wait timer and the one branch `main`. Then push to `main` once the delivery flag is `true`: the Stage code workflow runs and names the current code run in its parameter.
Alert email at bootstrap:
Nothing in this list has run against AWS. Each apply is the owner's. The list is part of the bootstrap, after the platform apply: the alerts root `infra/alerts` subscribes the run-failure alert address, from `.env`, to every alert topic the project creates: the platform alerts topic and the IAM stack's budget alerts topic. The project user has full permissions on those topics and their subscriptions (its SNS policy gives `sns:*` on their exact ARNs), so the project profile creates the subscriptions, and you click the confirmation link in each email. The root is not part of the platform stack and no pull request plan runs it, because the GitHub plan role never reads a subscription. Run every block from the repository root of the main checkout. Every block is a bash heredoc (paste it into the zsh terminal as it stands) that runs one call of the helper `scripts.infrastructure.alert_email` under `set -euo pipefail` and a fixed ERR trap that prints `step: stopped` for any exit status but 1 and 3. The helper reads `.env` and the Terraform outputs, checks every result, stops at the first failed or unexpected read or argument and prints status words only (`<subject>: <status>`): no ARN, no topic name, no account number, no address and no subscription identifier. Exit code 0 means the step is done, 1 means it stopped, and 3 means a subscription is still pending. The identity and exit status of every command it runs (never their output) go to the ignored file `plans/alert_email/last_run.log`, and the saved plans and the plan digest to the ignored folder `plans/alert_email`. The address stays in the ignored `.env` file and in the ignored rendered inputs. No tracked file and no log holds it. Until the administrator applies the project user's SNS policy (steps 2 and 3), the apply of step 8 fails with an access denied error.

1. Set the address in `.env` as `ALERT_EMAIL=<one address>`. One plain address only: no name, no list, no spaces. An empty or missing `ALERT_EMAIL` creates no subscription, so skip the rest of this list. The address reaches only the alerts root: the platform and services stacks never receive it.

2. Plan the project user's SNS policy (administrator profile). Set `ADMIN_PROFILE` to the administrator profile name first (`export ADMIN_PROFILE=...`). The policy file gives `sns:*` on the exact ARNs of the platform alerts topic, the budget alerts topic and their subscriptions. The helper stops if the plan holds a step for any policy but the SNS policy. It stores the `Plan digest` exactly as the plan printed it in `plans/alert_email/policy_digest.txt`:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email policy-plan --admin-profile "${ADMIN_PROFILE:-}"
BLOCK
```

3. Apply the SNS policy (administrator profile) with the stored digest and the typed confirmation. Apply changes nothing if the template or the live policy changed since the plan:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email policy-apply --admin-profile "${ADMIN_PROFILE:-}"
BLOCK
```

4. Plan the platform stack as in the platform step of the bootstrap (project profile). The stack creates the alerts topic and holds no subscription. If the bootstrap already applied it, the plan shows no change. The helper stops if the plan deletes or replaces anything:

```sh

set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email plan platform
BLOCK
```

5. Apply the platform stack (project profile). It applies exactly the plan of step 4 after the helper reads it again:

```sh

trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email apply platform
BLOCK
```

6. Check that Terraform reports the platform alerts topic and the IAM stack's budget alerts topic, and that both are the topics `.env` names:

Alert email teardown:
Nothing in this list has run against AWS. Each step is the owner's. Run every block from the repository root of the main checkout. Every block is a bash heredoc with the same strict options and fixed ERR trap as in the alert email list. It runs one call of the helper `scripts.infrastructure.alert_email`: the helper checks every result, stops at the first failed or unexpected read or argument and prints status words only (`<subject>: <status>`). Exit code 0 means the step is done, 1 means it stopped, and 3 means a subscription is still pending. The identity and exit status of every command (never their output) go to the ignored file `plans/alert_email/last_run.log`. Run this list before the platform stack and the IAM stack are removed: the alerts root reads the platform output when it renders its inputs. The project user destroys the subscriptions with the project profile and keeps everything else: the topics, the platform stack, `.env` and the state of the other stacks. The same steps apply when the alert address changes: run this list with the old address in place, change `ALERT_EMAIL` and run the alert email list again.

1. Read which subscriptions the alerts root state holds (project profile). A failed state read, or a resource other than the two subscriptions, stops the block:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email state
BLOCK
```

2. Plan the destroy of the alerts root (project profile). The plan must delete exactly the subscriptions that step 1 reported and nothing else; the helper stops on any other change:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email plan alerts --destroy
BLOCK
```

3. Apply the destroy plan (project profile). It applies exactly the plan of step 2 after the helper reads it again:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email apply alerts --destroy
BLOCK
```

4. Check that neither topic has a subscription of the address left (project profile). A subscription that is still pending was never confirmed: it delivers nothing and AWS expires it on its own, and the block ends with exit code 3. The teardown is not complete until a later run of this block reports `none` on both topics. A confirmed subscription that the state did not hold stops the block with exit code 1:

```sh
bash <<'BLOCK'
set -euo pipefail
trap 'code=$?; case "$code" in 1|3) ;; *) echo "step: stopped" ;; esac' ERR
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.infrastructure.alert_email subscriptions --expect none
BLOCK
```

5. Write the result, the subscriptions that remain and the ongoing cost (none) in the run record under `plans/alert_email`.
